entries.1:1: Paul opens by saying he is an apostle because God and Christ Jesus commanded it, not because he chose it himself. This reminds the reader that God is the Savior and Jesus is the one we hope in.
entries.1:2: Paul calls Timothy his true son in the faith, showing a close mentor relationship. He wishes him grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Jesus Christ.
entries.1:3: Paul reminds Timothy that he asked him to stay in Ephesus when Paul went on to Macedonia. His purpose was to stop certain people there from teaching wrong ideas.
entries.1:4: Paul wanted them to stop chasing made-up stories and endless family histories, which only create arguments. These distract from God's plan, which works through faith.
entries.1:5: The goal of Paul's instruction is love that comes from a pure heart, a good conscience, and sincere faith. This is what healthy teaching should produce in a person's life.
entries.1:6: Some people have wandered away from these things and turned to empty talk instead. It's a warning that drifting from love and faith leads to pointless speech.
entries.1:7: These people want to be teachers of the law but don't understand what they're saying or what they insist on so confidently. Wanting to teach isn't the same as being qualified to teach.
entries.1:8: Paul says the law itself is good, as long as it's used the right way. The problem isn't the law but how people misuse it.
entries.1:9: The law isn't aimed at good people but at lawbreakers, the rebellious, the ungodly, sinners, and those who kill their parents or others. It exists to restrain and expose evil.
entries.1:10: The law also addresses sexual sin, kidnapping, lying, and false promises, along with anything else that contradicts sound teaching. It shows what behavior doesn't fit with God's truth.
entries.1:11: This sound teaching matches the good news about the glory of the great God, which Paul was entrusted to guard and proclaim. The gospel and right living go together.
entries.1:12: Paul thanks Christ Jesus, who gave him strength and trusted him enough to appoint him to service. Even a former enemy of the church can be given a job by God.
entries.1:13: Paul admits he once insulted God, persecuted believers, and acted violently. But he received mercy because he acted ignorantly, without faith.
entries.1:14: The Lord's grace poured out abundantly on Paul, along with the faith and love that come through Christ Jesus. God's kindness was far greater than Paul's past.
entries.1:15: This saying is trustworthy and worth fully accepting: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, and Paul calls himself the worst of them. It's a reminder that no one is beyond God's rescue.
entries.1:16: Paul received mercy so that in him, the worst sinner, Christ could show his full patience as an example for everyone who would later believe and receive eternal life. God's mercy to one person gives hope to many.
entries.1:17: Paul breaks into praise to the eternal King, the immortal, invisible, only God, giving him honor and glory forever. It's a fitting response to the mercy just described.
entries.1:18: Paul gives Timothy this instruction in line with earlier prophetic words about him, so those words would strengthen him to fight well. Encouragement from others can help us stay faithful.
entries.1:19: Timothy is to hold on to faith and keep a good conscience. Some people have ignored their conscience and shipwrecked their faith.
entries.1:20: Paul names Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom he handed over to Satan so they would stop speaking against God. This was a serious step meant to correct them, not just punish them.
entries.2:1: Paul wants the church to pray for everyone, asking God for help and thanking him for people. This means no one is left out of our prayers, even people we don't know.
entries.2:2: He especially wants prayer for rulers and leaders, so that society stays peaceful and we can live calmly and honor God. Praying for those in power is part of a faithful life.
entries.2:3: Praying for all people, including leaders, is good and pleases God, who saves us. Our prayers for others matter to him.
entries.2:4: God wants every person to be saved and to come to know the truth. No one is beyond his desire to rescue, so we should pray with that same wide heart.
entries.2:5: There is only one God, and only one person who brings us to him: Jesus Christ, a real man. We come to God through Jesus alone, not through anything else.
entries.2:6: Jesus gave his own life as a payment for everyone, and in due time this was made known. His sacrifice is for all people, which is why we pray for all.
entries.2:7: Paul says he was appointed to announce this message and teach the non-Jewish nations the true faith. He insists he is telling the truth about his calling.
entries.2:8: Paul wants men everywhere to pray sincerely, with clean hands and hearts, without anger or quarreling. Prayer should come from a peaceful, honest heart.
entries.2:9: Women should dress modestly and with dignity, not showing off expensive hair styles, gold, pearls, or costly clothes. What you wear should reflect a serious, humble heart.
entries.2:10: Instead, women who honor God should be known for their good deeds. Character and kindness are the real adornment of a believer.
entries.2:11: A woman should learn quietly and with a teachable, respectful attitude. Learning is encouraged, but done in a humble way.
entries.2:12: Paul does not permit a woman to teach or to have authority over a man in the church, but to remain quiet. This is his instruction for order in the church at that time.
entries.2:13: Paul grounds his instruction in the order of creation: Adam was made first, and then Eve. He appeals to how God made things from the beginning.
entries.2:14: Adam was not the one deceived; the woman was tricked and fell into wrongdoing. Paul points to this as a reason for his caution about women teaching.
entries.2:15: Yet women will be kept safe through childbirth if they continue in faith, love, and holy self-control. God's care is promised to those who keep trusting and living rightly.
entries.3:1: Wanting to be a church leader is wanting a good and worthwhile job. It is fine to desire this role because it means serving others.
entries.3:2: A church leader must be someone people respect, faithful to his wife, calm, sensible, orderly, welcoming to guests, and able to teach. His life at home and in public should show he can be trusted.
entries.3:3: A leader must not be hot-tempered, violent, quarrelsome, or greedy for money. He should be gentle and fair with people.
entries.3:4: He must manage his own household well and keep his children respectful and under control. How he leads his family shows what kind of leader he will be.
entries.3:5: If a man cannot take care of his own family, he cannot be trusted to care for a whole church. Caring for people starts at home.
entries.3:6: A new believer should not become a leader too soon, or he may become proud and fall into the same trap as the devil. Growth and maturity take time.
entries.3:7: He must also have a good reputation with people outside the church. A bad name can bring shame on the church and leave him open to the devil's traps.
entries.3:8: Church servants must be serious and honest, not heavy drinkers or greedy for money. Their words and habits should match their faith.
entries.3:9: They must hold firmly to the truths of the faith with a clear conscience. Believing the right things goes together with living a clean life.
entries.3:10: They should be tested first, and only serve if nothing bad is found in them. Checking someone's character before giving them a role protects the church.
entries.3:11: The women serving in the church must be serious, not gossipers, self-controlled, and faithful in everything. Their conduct matters just as much as the men's.
entries.3:12: Church servants must be faithful to their wives and manage their children and households well. A stable home is a sign of reliable service.
entries.3:13: Those who serve well gain respect and grow confident in their faith in Christ. Good service builds them up and blesses the church.
entries.3:14: Paul is writing these instructions now, even though he hopes to visit soon. He wants the church to be prepared either way.
entries.3:15: If Paul is delayed, this letter shows how people should behave in God's household, the church. The church belongs to the living God and upholds the truth.
entries.3:16: The great truth of the faith is that Christ came as a man, was shown to be right by the Spirit, was seen by angels, preached to the nations, believed in around the world, and taken up in glory. This is the heart of what Christians believe.
entries.4:1: God's Spirit warns that in days to come some believers will abandon the faith by listening to deceptive spirits and false teachings. It means we should guard our beliefs, because not every spiritual message comes from God.
entries.4:2: These false teachers are hypocrites whose words cannot be trusted, and their consciences have grown so hard they no longer feel guilt. It reminds us that people can teach wrong things sincerely while being spiritually numb.
entries.4:3: These teachers forbid marriage and certain foods, even though God made these good things for believers to enjoy with thankfulness. It warns against anyone who adds rules God never made.
entries.4:4: Everything God created is good, and nothing should be rejected if we receive it with gratitude. It means we can enjoy God's gifts thankfully rather than treating ordinary things as evil.
entries.4:5: Food and other gifts are set apart for holy use when we remember God's word and pray over them. It encourages us to thank God and pray before enjoying what he provides.
entries.4:6: If you remind the believers of these truths, you will serve Christ Jesus well, nourished by the faith and sound teaching you have followed. It shows that good teaching strengthens both the teacher and the church.
entries.4:7: Stay away from pointless, silly myths and instead discipline yourself in godly living. It means we should spend our energy on what truly shapes our character.
entries.4:8: Physical exercise helps a little, but godliness benefits everything, holding promise for this life and the life to come. It means spiritual training matters more than bodily training, though both have value.
entries.4:9: This statement is trustworthy and deserves full acceptance by everyone. It means the promise about godliness is certain and worth building your life on.
entries.4:10: We work and struggle hard because our hope is in the living God, who saves all people and especially those who believe. It means our effort is worth it because God is faithful to those who trust him.
entries.4:11: Timothy is told to command and teach these things to the church. It means these truths are not optional suggestions but instructions to be passed on.
entries.4:12: Don't let anyone look down on you because you are young; instead, be an example in your speech, conduct, love, faith, and purity. It means your life can earn respect regardless of your age.
entries.4:13: Until Paul arrives, Timothy should devote himself to reading Scripture publicly, encouraging believers, and teaching. It means faithful ministry centers on God's word and building people up.
entries.4:14: Use the spiritual gift God gave you when the church leaders laid hands on you and prophesied over you. It means God gives each believer gifts to use, not to neglect.
entries.4:15: Be diligent about these things and throw yourself into them so everyone can see your progress. It means growth in faith takes effort and should be visible over time.
entries.4:16: Watch your own life and your teaching closely and keep at it, because doing so will bring salvation to you and to those who listen. It means our personal integrity and our message both matter for ourselves and others.
entries.5:1: Paul tells Timothy to treat older church leaders with respect, like a father, rather than speaking harshly to them. Readers should correct people gently and respectfully, especially those older or in authority.
entries.5:2: Older women should be treated like mothers and younger women like sisters, with pure motives. Readers should relate to people of the opposite sex with genuine family-like care and no improper thoughts.
entries.5:3: The church should care for widows who have no one else to support them. Readers should honor and help those who are truly alone and in need.
entries.5:4: If a widow has children or grandchildren, those relatives should take care of her rather than leaving it to the church. Readers should see caring for aging family members as a good and God-pleasing duty.
entries.5:5: A widow with no family puts her trust in God and spends her time in prayer. Readers can learn from her example of depending on God and praying persistently.
entries.5:6: A widow who lives only for pleasure is spiritually dead even while she is alive. Readers are warned that self-indulgence can destroy real spiritual life.
entries.5:7: Timothy is to teach these things clearly so no one can be criticized for wrong behavior. Readers should take such instructions seriously and live in a way that avoids blame.
entries.5:8: Anyone who neglects to provide for their own family has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever. Readers should see caring for their household as a basic Christian responsibility.
entries.5:9: Only widows who are at least sixty and were faithful to one husband should be put on the church's official list of widows. Readers should understand that the church's support was organized with careful standards.
entries.5:10: A widow qualifies by her good reputation and good deeds, such as raising children, welcoming strangers, and helping people in trouble. Readers should be known for practical kindness and service.
entries.5:11: Younger widows should not be put on the list, because desires can pull them away from their commitment to Christ and toward remarriage. Readers should be careful about making solemn commitments they may later abandon.
entries.5:12: Such women face judgment for breaking their earlier pledge of faith. Readers are reminded that promises made to God matter and should be kept.
entries.5:13: Younger widows on the list can become idle, going from house to house and gossiping about things they shouldn't. Readers should avoid laziness and meddling in other people's business.
entries.5:14: Paul wants younger widows to marry, have children, and manage their homes, so enemies have nothing bad to say. Readers should value stable family life and avoid giving critics a reason to speak against the faith.
entries.5:15: Some have already turned away to follow Satan. Readers are warned that drifting from faith is a real danger.
entries.5:16: If a Christian woman has widowed relatives, she should help them so the church isn't burdened and can help those truly alone. Readers should let family help family first, so the church can care for those with no one.
entries.5:17: Leaders who lead well deserve double honor, especially those who preach and teach. Readers should respect and support those who faithfully teach God's word.
entries.5:18: Scripture says workers deserve their pay, using the picture of an ox allowed to eat while it works. Readers should see that those who labor in ministry should be supported fairly.
entries.5:19: An accusation against a church leader should only be accepted if two or three witnesses confirm it. Readers should not believe or spread charges against leaders based on a single person's word.
entries.5:20: Those who keep sinning should be corrected publicly so others will be warned. Readers should understand that open sin may need open correction to protect the community.
entries.5:21: Paul solemnly commands Timothy, before God, Christ, and the angels, to follow these instructions without favoritism. Readers should act fairly and not show partiality in church matters.
entries.5:22: Don't lay hands on someone hastily to appoint them, or you share in their sins; keep yourself pure. Readers should be careful and not too quick to endorse or appoint people to ministry.
entries.5:23: Paul tells Timothy to drink a little wine for his stomach and frequent illnesses instead of only water. Readers can see that practical care for health is reasonable and not against faith.
entries.5:24: Some people's sins are obvious and lead them to judgment, while others' sins show up later. Readers should remember that hidden sin will eventually come to light.
entries.5:25: Good works are often visible, and even those that aren't obvious cannot stay hidden. Readers should keep doing good, knowing God sees and will bring it to light.
entries.6:1: Christian servants should treat their masters with full respect, so that people won't speak badly of God and the Christian message. Your everyday conduct can either honor or damage God's reputation.
entries.6:2: If a servant's master is also a Christian, the servant should respect him even more and serve well, because they are brothers in the faith. Paul tells Timothy to teach and enforce these instructions.
entries.6:3: Anyone who teaches something different from the healthy words of Jesus and the teaching that leads to godly living is off track. True teaching should match what Jesus said and produce a godly life.
entries.6:4: Such a person is proud and actually knows nothing; they are obsessed with arguments and word-fights, which stir up envy, conflict, insults, and suspicion. Fighting over words damages relationships rather than building them up.
entries.6:5: These people have corrupt minds and have lost touch with the truth, and they treat faith in God as a way to make money. Watch out for anyone who uses religion for personal profit.
entries.6:6: Real faith combined with contentment is a great gain. Being satisfied with what you have, alongside trusting God, is true wealth.
entries.6:7: We brought nothing into the world when we were born, and we can't take anything with us when we die. This reminds you that material things are temporary and shouldn't be your main focus.
entries.6:8: If we have food to eat and a place to live, we should be satisfied. Basic needs being met is enough reason for contentment.
entries.6:9: People who long to be rich fall into temptation and get trapped by many foolish and harmful desires that lead to ruin and destruction. Chasing wealth puts you in spiritual danger.
entries.6:10: The love of money is a root of all kinds of evil, and some who have craved it have wandered from the faith and caused themselves great pain. Money itself isn't the problem, but loving it leads people away from God.
entries.6:11: As a man of God, Timothy should run from these things and instead pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance, and gentleness. You should actively chase good character rather than just avoid evil.
entries.6:12: Fight the good fight of faith and hold on to eternal life, which you were called to and which you publicly confessed before many witnesses. Your faith is worth struggling for, and your public commitment matters.
entries.6:13: Paul solemnly charges Timothy in the presence of God, who gives life to everything, and of Christ Jesus, who made a good confession before Pontius Pilate. This shows the seriousness of the command and the example Jesus set.
entries.6:14: Keep the command without spot or blame until our Lord Jesus Christ appears. You are to stay faithful and morally clean while you wait for Christ's return.
entries.6:15: God will reveal Christ at the proper time—he is the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords. God is in control of timing and is above every earthly power.
entries.6:16: God alone has immortality and dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has seen or can see; to him be honor and eternal power. God is far greater and holier than we can fully grasp, and he deserves all honor.
entries.6:17: Tell those who are rich in this world not to be arrogant or to put their hope in uncertain wealth, but in God, who richly provides everything for our enjoyment. Wealth is unreliable; God is the one you can trust.
entries.6:18: The rich should do good, be rich in good works, be generous, and be willing to share. Wealth should be used to bless others, not just yourself.
entries.6:19: By doing this they store up a good foundation for the future, so they can take hold of true life. Generosity now builds something lasting for eternity.
entries.6:20: Timothy, guard what has been entrusted to you, and turn away from godless chatter and the opposing arguments of what is falsely called knowledge. Protect the true faith from empty and misleading ideas.
entries.6:21: Some who have pursued this false knowledge have wandered away from the faith. Paul closes with a wish that grace be with them, reminding us that wrong ideas can pull people away from trusting God.
